common_name: ColorBlaze Kingswood Torch Coleus (Tall Striped Shade Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Kingswood Torch is a Proven Winners ColorBlaze coleus bred for a tall, upright habit and striking striped foliage, performing best with morning sun and afternoon shade in a hot Gulf South summer.

directions: Plant in partial sun to full shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix, giving it morning sun and afternoon shade for the best performance in a hot climate; Kingswood Torch is a tall, vigorous coleus in the Proven Winners ColorBlaze series, bearing burgundy foliage boldly striped with chartreuse and cherry-red down the center of each leaf, creating a flame-like effect that gives the cultivar its name. Its upright, three-foot habit makes it a strong thriller plant for the back of a shaded container or border rather than a low edging plant. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy in foliage production, and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage fuller branching and prevent the tall stems from becoming leggy.

common_name: Alexander's Great Brunnera (Giant Silver Heartleaf Brunnera)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Alexander's Great is a Terra Nova Nurseries introduction from an exceptionally large-leaved seedling found by Belarusian plantsman Alexander Zukeivich, producing markedly bigger silvered leaves than the widely grown Jack Frost.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Alexander's Great is a giant-leaved brunnera selection bred to outsize the popular Jack Frost cultivar, with broad, heart-shaped leaves heavily overlaid in reflective silver and traced with contrasting green veining, brightening a dark shade bed on a bolder scale than standard brunnera. In spring, sprays of small azure-blue forget-me-not flowers rise above the emerging foliage before the leaves reach full size. Like other brunnera, it needs consistent moisture and will scorch in dry soil or hot afternoon sun, so mulch well and provide reliable shade in a Gulf South summer. It is propagated only by division, since named brunnera cultivars do not come true from seed.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, organically rich soil in shade to dappled shade; Chocolate Shogun was bred by Japanese astilbe breeder Nagasaki Teruhisa and tolerates somewhat more sun than most astilbe cultivars provided soil moisture stays consistent.

directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1-2 inches below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in shade to dappled shade; Chocolate Shogun stands out among astilbe cultivars for its glossy, deeply serrated, chocolate-bronze foliage, which provides rich color contrast in the shade garden even before the plumes appear. In summer it sends up airy, feathery plumes blushed white to soft pink above the dark foliage. Astilbe does not tolerate drought and will brown and decline quickly without steady moisture, so mulch well and water regularly through the growing season, especially in a hot, humid Gulf South summer. Leave the dried plumes standing through fall and winter for ornamental interest, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Bronze Peacock arose as a tissue-culture mutation of Rodgersia pinnata 'Ideal' and has the darkest foliage of any rodgersia cultivar, though it needs more shade and moisture in the Gulf South than in cooler climates to avoid leaf scorch.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, along a pond edge or in a damp woodland bed; Bronze Peacock is grown primarily for its foliage, producing large, glossy, deeply bronze-brown palmate leaves that are the darkest of any rodgersia cultivar available, standing out dramatically against greener shade-garden companions. In summer it sends up plumes of small pink flowers above the foliage, similar to an astilbe, but the bronze leaves remain the main attraction through the season. It needs reliably moist, even boggy soil to perform well and will scorch or wilt in dry conditions, so a spot near a water feature or low, damp corner of the garden suits it best. In hot Southern climates give it more shade than the mostly-sun exposure it tolerates further north, since intense summer sun combined with humidity stress can damage the foliage.

common_name: Younique Salmon Astilbe (Early-Blooming Heavy Shade Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, organically rich soil in shade; Younique Salmon is a Dutch-bred astilbe from the Younique series noted for unusually good tolerance of heavy shade and for blooming about two weeks earlier than standard astilbe cultivars.

directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1-2 inches below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in shade; Younique Salmon is bred to tolerate deeper shade than most astilbe cultivars, making it a useful option for the darker corners of a woodland or shaded bed where other astilbe struggle. It produces soft salmon-pink plumes roughly two weeks earlier in the season than standard astilbe, extending the shade garden's early-summer bloom display, and the spent flower heads dry to an attractive caramel-tan color that provides continued interest into winter if left standing. Astilbe does not tolerate drought, so mulch well and water consistently, especially through a hot Gulf South summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.
